subtopics: Marconi's December 1901 Signal Hill St. John's Newfoundland experiment: exact dates, equipment used (coherer, antenna, kite/balloon aerials), what signal was claimed to be received (Morse letter 'S' from Poldhu, Cornwall)

Evidence supporting Marconi's 1901 transatlantic reception claim: witness testimony (Kemp, Paget), Marconi's notebooks, 1902 follow-up experiments, 1923 Poldhu–Signal Hill re-enactment with period equipment
Scientific and technical challenges to Marconi's 1901 claim: physics of ~820 kHz daytime propagation, D-layer absorption, signal-to-noise arguments, atmospheric noise, skeptics' critiques
First confirmed transatlantic radio transmission and reliable two-way service: Marconi's 1902 Glace Bay Cape Breton station, 1902/1903 tests, when transatlantic wireless was definitively established
Historians' assessments of the 1901 Signal Hill claim: Sungook Hong, W.J. Baker, Huw Williams, 2001 centenary debates, IEEE and academic literature
Role of the ionosphere (Kennelly-Heaviside layer) discovery in explaining transatlantic propagation and how it validates or undermines the 1901 account
Alternative or earlier claimants to transatlantic wireless communication: Nikola Tesla's claims, Oliver Lodge, other contemporaries before or around 1901
Modern technical analyses, simulations, and replication studies of the December 1901 Poldhu-to-Signal-Hill experiment, including centenary modeling studies and their conclusions
